analysis: The PR replaces the fixed ExponentialBackoff in CoordinatorClient+Connection.runLoop (head lines 12-53) with an injectable CoordinatorReconnectPolicy. The policy decides each delay from the session's open duration and the coordinator's WebSocket close code. It adds CoordinatorSessionRecorder (CoordinatorClientState.swift head ~500-527), a lock-protected recorder of open time and close code. CoordinatorClient.swift only adds the reconnectPolicy init parameter and stored property. connectAndRun and receiveLoop keep the same handshake, registration, App Attest resume nonce handling, chunk-writer binding, and defer teardown. Examined: the receive callback records the close code on connectionQueue and does not alter frame handling. Close frames still throw connectionClosed, so a malformed or hostile close payload only feeds sentCloseCode (head 513-522), which reads the first two bytes after a count>=2 guard and cannot crash. Reconnect timing is now influenced by coordinator-supplied close codes. The coordinator is trusted, so this is not an adversary-controlled input. A malicious provider gains nothing, since the policy runs on its own client. Availability and DoS properties (T-010, T-057) depend on CoordinatorReconnectPolicy, whose implementation was not supplied. The questions are whether it enforces a nonzero minimum delay, a bounded maximum, and anti-thrash behavior after a short-lived session or close code 1012. The `TimeInterval.random(in:)` call could trap if the range is empty or inverted; that is a robustness question, not evidenced here. The logs now include close_code, which is non-sensitive. The session recorder holds no secrets. The App Attest resume nonce and the authorization lifecycle (T-053) are unchanged. No security regression is identified in the supplied source. The reconnect policy file remains an unverified contract for the next pass.
